description: Tasks for the first 2 weeks after death. Focus: Handle true emergencies first, then stabilize. Most things can wait—these can't.

tasks.title: Handle the body / contact funeral home
tasks.description: If death happened at home: call hospice (if enrolled) or 911. They'll pronounce death. Hospital handles this if they died there. Then call a funeral home—they come get the body and guide you.
tasks.why_now: This literally must happen first. The body needs to be taken care of.
tasks.why_it_matters: This is the first thing that needs to happen. The funeral home will pick up the body and help you through the initial steps. You don't need a full plan yet—just someone to call.
tips: If death happened at home with hospice: call the hospice number first—they'll guide you
If death happened at home without hospice: call 911—they'll pronounce death
If death happened at hospital: the hospital staff will guide you
You don't need to have chosen a funeral home yet—any one can pick up the body
If there were pre-planned arrangements, find those first

tasks.title: Order death certificates
tasks.description: The funeral home does this for you. Order 10-15 certified copies. They cost $10-25 each but you'll need them for banks, insurance, government, everything.
tasks.why_now: You cannot do anything else—close accounts, file insurance claims, access funds—without certified death certificates. Everything depends on this.
tasks.why_it_matters: Banks, insurance companies, government agencies all require certified copies. Getting enough upfront saves time. Order more than you think you need—10-15 is typical.
tips: The funeral home can order these for you—this is the easiest way
Order 10-15 copies minimum—more if the estate is complex
Certified copies cost $10-25 each depending on the state
Keep track of which institutions keep the certificate vs. return it
You can order more later from vital records, but it takes longer

tasks.title: Call one person who can help make calls
tasks.description: You don't have to do this alone. Call one trusted person—sibling, friend, anyone—who can help notify others. You don't have to make every call yourself.
tasks.why_now: You're in shock. Having someone help spread the word means you don't have to repeat the hardest conversation 20 times.
tasks.why_it_matters: Sharing the burden of notifications protects your energy for the decisions only you can make. One person can create a phone tree to reach everyone.
tips: Ask this person to help notify extended family and friends
It's okay to text or email instead of calling everyone
You don't have to have all the details—'I don't know yet' is fine
Consider a phone tree where each person calls 2-3 others
It's okay to not answer your phone right now

tasks.title: Take care of their pets
tasks.description: If they had pets at their home, someone needs to care for them. Permanent arrangements can wait—just make sure they're fed and safe.
tasks.why_now: Pets can't wait. They need food, water, and care. Permanent decisions about them can come later.
tasks.why_it_matters: Pets need immediate care. Making permanent arrangements can wait, but their basic needs cannot.
tips: Just focus on immediate care—feeding, walking, medication if needed
Ask a family member or neighbor to help temporarily
Locate veterinary records for any ongoing medications
Permanent arrangements can wait until you're ready
Pets can be a source of comfort during grief
tasks.can_wait_message: Permanent arrangements for pets can wait—just ensure their basic needs are met now.

tasks.title: Secure their home
tasks.description: If they lived alone: lock up, adjust thermostat (prevent frozen pipes), check for perishables, collect mail. Hold off on cleaning anything out.
tasks.why_now: An empty house can be targeted (especially after obituaries are published). Basic security and prevention of damage.
tasks.why_it_matters: Home break-ins after a death do happen, especially when obituaries reveal funeral times. Basic security protects belongings and prevents damage.
tips: Lock all doors and windows
Set lights on timers to make the home look occupied
Adjust thermostat to prevent frozen pipes or excessive humidity
Collect mail regularly—piled up mail signals an empty home
Don't start cleaning out or sorting belongings yet—that can wait
tasks.can_wait_message: Cleaning out the house can wait. Just secure it for now.

tasks.title: Find the important papers
tasks.description: You're hunting now because you need them: will, insurance policies, bank statements, deed, anything official. Check: filing cabinet, desk, safe, safe deposit box, email.
tasks.why_now: You need to find the will to know who's in charge. You need insurance policies to file claims. Gather now—act later.
tasks.why_it_matters: These documents guide everything else: who's the executor, what assets exist, what insurance can be claimed. You're gathering information, not making decisions yet.
tips: Check: filing cabinet, desk drawers, home safe, closet boxes
Look for a safe deposit box key—check their wallet and keychain
Search email for 'policy', 'account', 'statement', attorney names
Check mail for recent statements from banks or insurance companies
Ask surviving spouse or siblings if they know where things are

tasks.title: Figure out if there's a will
tasks.description: This tells you who's legally in charge (the executor). Check the papers you found, ask surviving parent, search email for 'attorney' or 'estate'. No will = intestate probate.
tasks.why_now: The will names the executor—the person legally authorized to manage the estate. Without knowing this, you don't know who can make decisions.
tasks.why_it_matters: The executor named in the will has legal authority over the estate. If there's no will (intestate), the court will appoint an administrator—usually next of kin.
tips: Check the documents you gathered for anything labeled 'Last Will'
Ask if they had an attorney who might have a copy
Check their email for any law firm names
No will doesn't mean no inheritance—it just means state rules apply
The will may also contain burial wishes—check if there's time

tasks.title: Notify their employer (if working)
tasks.description: Call HR. Ask about: final paycheck, life insurance through work, 401k/pension, COBRA for any dependents. HR handles this regularly—they'll tell you what they need.
tasks.why_now: The employer may owe final wages and may have life insurance you don't know about. Many people have employer-provided life insurance.
tasks.why_it_matters: Employers often provide life insurance as a benefit that families forget about. There may also be final pay, vacation payout, pension or 401k benefits.
documents_needed: Death certificate (may be needed later for benefits)
tips: Ask about any life insurance through the employer—this is common
Ask about 401(k) or pension benefits and how to claim them
Ask about COBRA health insurance if there are dependents
Request any personal items from their workspace
Ask about unpaid wages, vacation time, or bonuses owed

tasks.title: Notify Social Security
tasks.description: Call 1-800-772-1213 or the funeral home may do this for you—ask. Benefits stop. Surviving spouse may qualify for survivor benefits.
tasks.why_now: Benefits paid after death must be returned. Better to notify quickly. Surviving spouse benefits must be applied for.
tasks.why_it_matters: Social Security benefits stop at death and any payments received after must be returned. A surviving spouse may be eligible for survivor benefits—potentially up to 100% of the deceased's benefit.
documents_needed: Surviving spouse's Social Security number (if applying for survivor benefits)
tips: The funeral home often reports the death—ask if they did
Benefits are not prorated—the full month's payment must be returned
Survivor benefits must be applied for—they're not automatic
A surviving spouse can receive benefits as early as age 60

tasks.title: Find out about life insurance
tasks.description: Check papers you gathered, their email, bank statements for premium payments. Ask employer about group coverage. These claims can be filed soon and pay within weeks.
tasks.why_now: Life insurance claims typically pay within 2-4 weeks of filing. This money may be needed for funeral costs or family support.
tasks.why_it_matters: Life insurance provides funds quickly and doesn't go through probate. Many policies go unclaimed because families don't know they exist.
tips: Check the documents you gathered for any insurance policies
Search email for insurance company names
Check bank statements for premium payment deductions
Ask employer about group life insurance coverage
Check for coverage through professional associations or credit cards

tasks.title: Give yourself permission to pause
tasks.description: You don't have to do everything this week. Banks aren't going anywhere. Bills can be late. The only true urgencies are: the body, death certificates, and preventing damage to an empty home.
tasks.why_now: You're in shock and grief. Most things can wait even if they feel urgent.
tasks.why_it_matters: In the fog of grief, everything feels urgent. Most things aren't. Taking care of yourself is not optional—it's required.
tips: The only true urgencies: body/funeral home, death certificates, securing the home
Banks, accounts, bills—all of this can wait a few days or even weeks
Don't pay their bills from your own money—there's no rush
It's okay to let calls go to voicemail
Eating, sleeping, and breathing come first
